nodes.statement: The rigid family is defined by a linear subspace of functions with fixed basis coefficients, inducing a rank-deficient Hessian at the solution; this algebraic structure ensures that the solution set dimension remains constant regardless of w, implying N_c(w) = O(1) for sufficiently wide networks.

The solution space of the rigid family corresponds to a low-dimensional manifold embedded in the function space, with vanishing curvature and geodesic stability under perturbation; this geometric rigidity implies that small-width networks can traverse the manifold efficiently to satisfy all constraints, yielding N_c(w) independent of w.

The optimization landscape of the rigid family exhibits a unique global minimum with a well-conditioned Hessian, enabling gradient-based methods to converge to zero-violation solutions even with small network widths; this implies N_c(w) remains bounded as w increases, unlike the fat family which has a flat, multi-modal landscape requiring large widths to escape local minima.

The held-out error distribution for the rigid family converges to a degenerate point mass at zero as $w$ increases, with variance decaying as $O(w^{-1})$, whereas the fat family exhibits heavy-tailed error distributions with non-vanishing variance, making $N_c(w)$ statistically ill-defined for the fat case.

The computational complexity of finding a zero-violation solution for the rigid family scales as $O(w \cdot \log h)$ using gradient-based optimization, while the fat family requires exponential time $O(2^w)$ in the worst case due to the high-dimensional search space, making $N_c(w)$ practically inaccessible for large $w$.

The solution manifold of the rigid family has a curvature bounded away from zero, ensuring that gradient descent converges linearly to a global minimum with a condition number $\kappa \leq C$ independent of $w$, whereas the fat family's manifold develops flat regions with $\kappa \to \infty$ as $w$ grows, causing optimization to stall.
